newsitem.title: UK: BOXING-BRITISH PAPERS EXPRESS REVULSION OVER TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-BRITISH PAPERS EXPRESS REVULSION OVER TYSON.

text.p: British newspapers on Monday punched out front-page headlines such as "Savage" and "Ban the beast" to express revulsion at Mike Tyson turning his world title bout against Evander Holyfield into a bloody ear-chewing battle.

"World Chomp -- Tyson chews ear off," declared the top-selling Sun tabloid, which devoted all of its first five pages and three sports pages to reports, pictures and comment on boxing's night of shame in Las Vegas.
The Sun carried a picture of Tyson biting one of champion Holyfield's ears on its main sports page with the headline: "Beast Tyson must never fight again".
"Boxing must not be dragged down by his animal bloodlust. Tyson must be banned from the ring for good," the tabloid said in an editorial.
The Daily Express headlined its front-page story: "Savage -- World-wide revulsion as Tyson bites off opponent's ear and takes boxing to new depths of depravity."
The Times' boxing correspondent Srikumar Sen said in his report from Las Vegas: "Mike Tyson's behaviour in the ring in the early hours here yesterday morning will leave an indelible stain on boxing.

"He is not only guilty of the worst crime in the sport, that of casting aside the rules and resorting to street fighting, he is also the most recognisable sportsman, if that is the word for him, in the world.
"Viewed by millions of families across the world, his act, which started like a caress, ended up as one of the most horrific actions witnessed in an event going under the banner of sport."

The Guardian's ringside correspondent Richard Williams said: "By stripping away the thin veneer of civilised behaviour which generally keeps prize fighting within the accepted bounds of professional sport, Tyson turned this into the most demeaning, not to say disgusting, night in the history of the heavyweight championship."

Referee Mills Lane disqualified Tyson before the start of the fourth round of Saturday night's bout after the challenger twice bit Holyfield's ears. The champion lost a small chunk from his right ear from the first bite and will have to undergo reconstructive surgery after doctors were unable to re-attach the torn flesh.

The Nevada State Athletic Commission, which regulates boxing in the state, was to hold an emergency meeting on Tuesday to decide whether to fine Tyson or suspend his licence for his behaviour in what had been an eagerly awaited rematch with Holyfield for the World Boxing Association heavyweight title.
The Nevada legislature's Senate Judiciary Committee met on Sunday morning and voted to amend its "unarmed combat legislation", which covers boxing.
Under the new rules, ear biting will be banned and may result in a fine of up to 50 percent of a fighter's purse. Up till now, they could fine Tyson only 10 percent of his $30 million fee.
Tyson became the youngest world heavyweight champion at the age of 20.
